3-5.title: How Plants Move Water
3-5.titleEs: Cómo las plantas mueven el agua
3-5.speaker: Ms. Rivera, science teacher

keyWords.def: plant parts under the ground
the part of a plant that holds it up
the dirt where plants grow

talk: Today we will learn how plants move water from the ground up to their leaves.
First, the roots take in water from the soil. Roots are like tiny straws under the ground.
Next, the water moves up through the stem. The stem has thin tubes inside it.
Then, the water reaches the leaves. The leaves use water and sunlight to make food for the plant.
I grow tomatoes in my garden, and they get very thirsty in the summer.
Finally, some water leaves the plant through tiny holes in the leaves. It goes out into the air.
So a plant moves water along one long path, from the roots to the stem to the leaves.

3-5.title: A Mail Carrier's Day
3-5.speaker: Mr. Okafor, mail carrier

keyWords.def: the building where mail is sorted and sent
the path someone follows every day
a box where mail is left for a home
the people who live in one area

talk: Hello, class. I am a mail carrier, and today I will tell you about my job.
First, I go to the post office early in the morning. I pick up the letters and boxes for my route.
Next, I put the mail in order by street and house number. This helps me work fast.
Then, I drive my truck and walk to each home. I put the mail in each mailbox, and I carry big boxes to the door.
My favorite part of the day is saying hello to a friendly dog named Pepper.
Finally, I take the letters that people want to send back to the post office.
Mail carriers help people in the community stay connected.

3-5.title: Measuring with a Ruler
3-5.speaker: Mr. Haddad, math teacher

keyWords.def: to find out how long or big something is
a standard amount, like an inch or a centimeter
not straight

talk: Today I will explain how to measure an object with a ruler.
First, put one end of the object at the zero mark on the ruler. Many rulers have a small space before zero, so look carefully.
Next, keep the object straight along the ruler. If the object is crooked, your number will be wrong.
Then, look at where the other end of the object stops. Read the number on the ruler at that spot.
My ruler is blue, and I have had it since I was in third grade.
Finally, write the number and the unit, like six inches or ten centimeters. A number without a unit does not tell the whole story.

3-5.title: The Girl Who Shared Her Seeds
3-5.titleEs: La niña que compartió sus semillas
3-5.speaker: Ms. Abara, reading teacher

keyWords.def: an old story people tell again and again
a very small town
small parts you plant to grow new plants

talk: Today I will tell you a short folktale called The Girl Who Shared Her Seeds.
Long ago, a girl named Lina lived in a small village. She had one bag of corn seeds.
First, Lina planted some seeds in her own garden. Next, she gave a handful of seeds to every family in the village.
I love this story because my grandmother told it to me when I was little.
Then, a big storm knocked down every plant in Lina's garden. But the corn in her neighbors' fields grew tall.
Finally, the neighbors shared their corn with Lina, because she had shared with them.
The lesson of the story is that when we share, others share with us.

6-8.title: What Causes Erosion
6-8.speaker: Dr. Patel, earth science teacher

keyWords.def: the process that moves rock and soil from one place to another
a huge, slow-moving mass of ice
a deep valley with steep sides
in the direction a river flows

talk: Today we will explore erosion, the process that moves rock and soil from one place to another. Three natural forces cause most erosion.
First, moving water is the strongest cause of erosion. Rivers carry sand and small rocks downstream, and over millions of years they can carve deep canyons.
In addition, wind causes erosion, especially in dry places with few plants. Strong wind picks up loose sand and blows it against rocks, slowly wearing them down.
Ice is the third cause. Glaciers are huge, slow rivers of ice that scrape the land and push rocks along as they move.
For example, the Great Lakes between the United States and Canada were dug out by glaciers long ago.
By the way, I took a photo of a glacier on a trip once, and my fingers almost froze.
However, people can slow erosion. Plant roots hold soil in place, so planting trees and grasses helps protect hillsides.
Understanding these forces helps communities protect their land and homes.

6-8.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
6-8.titleEs: Cómo un proyecto de ley se convierte en ley
6-8.speaker: Mr. Torres, civics teacher

keyWords.def: an idea for a new law that is written down
the part of government that makes laws, made of the House and the Senate
a small group that studies something closely
to reject a bill so it does not become a law

talk: Today I will explain how a bill becomes a law in the United States. A bill is an idea for a new law.
First, a member of Congress introduces the bill in either the House of Representatives or the Senate.
Next, a small group called a committee studies the bill. The committee can change it, approve it, or stop it.
After that, the full House or Senate debates the bill and votes on it. If most members vote yes, the bill goes to the other part of Congress, and the same steps happen again.
Fun fact, the first time I visited the Capitol building, I got lost looking for the cafeteria.
Finally, the bill goes to the President. If the President signs it, the bill becomes a law.
However, the President can veto, or reject, the bill. Congress can still pass it if two thirds of the House and two thirds of the Senate vote yes.
As a result, making a law takes many steps, and both Congress and the President play a role.

6-8.title: Ratios in Recipes
6-8.speaker: Ms. Nguyen, math teacher

keyWords.def: a comparison of two amounts
directions for making a food or drink
the amount of food made at one time
to make a number a certain number of times bigger

talk: Today we will use ratios to change the size of a recipe. A ratio compares two amounts.
For example, a lemonade recipe uses two cups of lemon juice for every six cups of water. The ratio of juice to water is two to six, which is the same as one to three.
First, decide how much you want to make. Suppose you want to make twice as much lemonade for a class party.
Next, multiply both amounts by the same number. Two times two is four cups of juice, and six times two is twelve cups of water.
However, if you add more water but no more juice, the ratio changes. As a result, the lemonade will taste weaker.
I once made lemonade for my family with way too much sugar, and my little brother loved it.
In addition, you can make a smaller batch by dividing both amounts by the same number.
The key idea is that equal ratios keep a recipe tasting the same, no matter the size of the batch.

6-8.title: A Longer Lunch Break
6-8.titleEs: Un recreo de almuerzo más largo
6-8.speaker: Jamal, student council member

keyWords.def: moving your body to stay healthy
to keep your attention on one thing
to agree with and help an idea

talk: Good morning, everyone. I believe our school should make the lunch break fifteen minutes longer.
First, students need time to move. Exercise helps our bodies stay healthy, and it helps our brains get ready to learn.
In addition, a break gives students time to make friends and solve problems together. For example, last week my friends and I worked out the rules for a new game without any adult help.
By the way, the pizza at lunch last Friday was really good.
On the other hand, some teachers worry that a longer break means less time for class.
However, many teachers notice that students focus better after a break. A short rest can help the next lesson go more smoothly, so the class time is used well.
As a result, I think a longer lunch break would help students be healthier, kinder, and better learners. Please support this idea at the next school meeting.
